narrative:
The model estimated a 64% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means it judged failure more likely than passing, and because your law-school application was assessed against that risk, you were denied admission. This is a probability, not a certainty.

The strongest reason was your third-year class-rank decile of 4, which is below the 5.79 average among accepted students. That lower third-year standing pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your LSAT score of 38.5, above the accepted average of 37.18, was the next most influential factor, but it pushed toward passing and was not enough to offset the academic-standing concern. Your first-year decile of 6 matched the accepted average, yet it still acted as a modest factor toward failure rather than a strength.

To move forward, ask admissions whether you can submit updated grades or an explanation for the third-year dip, and work with an advisor on a concrete academic-improvement plan. Consider applying again after strengthening your third-year record, and use your LSAT result as supporting evidence of readiness rather than the sole basis for appeal.
